title: Above everything, and nearest when your head is lowest
subtitle: Al-Aliyy: the Most High in essence, in rank and in power
intro: Al-Aliyy (الْعَلِيُّ) means The Most High: Allah is above all things in His essence, highest in rank and perfection, and above all in power, so nothing is ever over Him. Muslims declare it with their foreheads on the ground. It cures the urge to rise over others, and it shows the strange truth that bowing low brings you closest to Him.

root.sense: 'Uluw is height: being physically high, then being high in standing, control and say. It can be praised or blamed. The Quran says Pharaoh made himself high in the land (28:4), a height built on crushing others. Al-Aliyy is height that is real and rightful: no one stands above Him in any sense.

picture.label: Three ways He is Most High

row.title: Rise by lowering yourself to Him

knowing: Scholars explain that Al-Aliyy is high in three ways. {idea}He is above His creation in His essence, in a way that befits His majesty; He is highest in rank, with every attribute perfect; and He is highest in power, overcoming everything and overcome by nothing{/idea}. The early Muslims affirmed this as Allah described Himself, without asking how and without likening Him to anything created, and turned their attention to what it should change in them.

Al-Aliyy is not the same as Al-Muta'ali. Al-Aliyy is the fact of His highness, permanent and complete. Al-Muta'ali adds the sense of One who rises far above every likeness to creation and every flaw people attribute to Him. Nor is it the same as Al-Azim: one name speaks of height, the other of weight and magnitude. The Quran joins them at the close of Ayat al-Kursi: He is the Most High, the Magnificent (2:255).

Every claim to height by creatures is temporary and borrowed. {trap}Pharaoh's height ended in the sea{/trap}, and the Quran promises the Home of the Hereafter to those who do not seek height on earth or corruption (28:83).
seeing: The Arabic word tasbih, glorifying, is related to sabaha, to swim or float. Push a swimmer down and let go, and he rises back to the surface. When people insult Allah, deny Him or ascribe partners and children to Him, they are trying to drag Him down. Glorifying Him means declaring that He stays exactly where He is, Most High, while those who tried to lower Him only lowered themselves.

The Quran also joins Al-Aliyy with Al-Kabir when it describes the end of every false claim: the judgment belongs to Allah, the Most High, the Great (40:12), and when terror leaves the hearts of the angels at His word, they say He is the Most High, the Great (34:23).
trusting: In sujud, the highest part of your body, the face, touches the lowest place, the ground, and there you say Subhana Rabbiyal A'la: glory be to my Lord, the Most High (Sahih Muslim). The posture says everything: I am low, You are high. And then the surprise. {reward}The Prophet ﷺ said the closest a servant comes to his Lord is while prostrating, so make plenty of dua there (Sahih Muslim).{/reward} A king makes you bow to keep you at a distance. Al-Aliyy makes you bow to bring you near.

So take your hardest worries into sujud. A failing exam, a strained marriage, a debt that keeps growing: say them to the Most High with your forehead on the floor. {idea}Nothing that weighs on you is above Him, and nothing you say down there goes unheard.{/idea}
loving: Love grows where there is nearness, and here the Most High offers nearness through the lowest posture a person can take. {reward}The heart falls in love with Al-Aliyy because His highness does not push you away; it lifts you the moment you bow.{/reward} A companion once asked the Prophet ﷺ for his company in Paradise, and was told to help him with many prostrations (Sahih Muslim).
now: You have been passed over for promotion, and the one who got it boasts in the group chat. You feel small and want to prove yourself. {idea}Height that comes from climbing over people is Pharaoh's kind; Al-Aliyy offers a better kind.{/idea} Tonight, add two units of voluntary prayer and lengthen the sujud, and leave the climbing to Him.
old: Being high means being above other people in status and respect.
new: Only Al-Aliyy is truly high, and I rise closest to Him when my forehead touches the ground.
try: In your next prayer, make one sujud longer than usual and ask for one specific thing in your own words.

dua.text: Ya Aliyy, glory be to You, my Lord, the Most High. My face is on the ground before You; raise my heart to You, lower my pride, and answer me from Your highness with Your mercy.
dua.note: The Prophet ﷺ said Subhana Rabbiyal A'la in every prostration (Sahih Muslim), following the command of 87:1 to glorify the name of your Lord, the Most High.

pairs.why: They close Ayat al-Kursi together: Al-Aliyy is His height above all, Al-Azim the tremendous weight of His greatness.
Paired in 22:62, 31:30, 34:23 and 40:12: the Most High and the Great, height and greatness that no one shares.
He is Most High, yet He answers whoever calls Him: His highness never makes Him distant from His servants.

faq.a: Al-Aliyy means The Most High. Scholars explain that Allah is high in three ways: in His essence above His creation, in His rank and perfect attributes, and in His power over everything. No one and nothing is ever above Him.

faq.q: What is the difference between Al-Aliyy and Al-Muta'ali?
faq.a: Al-Aliyy describes His highness as a permanent, complete attribute. Al-Muta'ali, from a form that conveys transcendence, stresses that He is exalted far above any likeness to creation and above every defect people attribute to Him. Al-Muta'ali appears once in the Quran, in 13:9.

faq.q: Why do we say Subhana Rabbiyal A'la in sujud?
faq.a: Because the Prophet ﷺ said it in prostration, as reported in Sahih Muslim, echoing 87:1, glorify the name of your Lord, the Most High. In the lowest posture we declare His highness, and the Prophet ﷺ taught that this is when a servant is closest to Allah.

faq.q: Is Al-Aliyy the same as Al-A'la?
faq.a: They share a root and meaning. Al-Aliyy is the Most High; Al-A'la, used in 87:1, is the comparative form, the Highest, higher than anything else. Both declare that nothing is above Allah in essence, rank or power.
